newsitem.title: USA: Betty Shabazz, widow of Malcolm X, dies from burns.
newsitem.headline: Betty Shabazz, widow of Malcolm X, dies from burns.

text.p: Betty Shabazz, widow of slain civil rights leader Malcolm X, died on Monday from severe burns suffered in a fire allegedly set by her grandson.

Shabazz, 63, who became an educator and activist after her husband's murder, was burned on more than 80 percent of her body in the June 1 blaze, and doctors performed five skin-graft operations in hopes of saving her life.
She died at 2:46 p.m. (1846 GMT) at Jacobi Medical Centre in the Bronx with family members at her side, a hospital spokeswoman said.
Police say her troubled 12-year-old grandson Malcolm, named after his grandfather, set the blaze with gasoline in his grandmother's apartment in Mount Vernon, New York.
Shabazz' six daughters met with reporters outside the hospital after their mother's death.
"My father lived strong, my mother did honourably, and her daughters are going to go through a lot," said the eldest, Attallah, the only one to speak publicly.
"Betty Shabazz has made a transition," she added. "But she is very mighty where she is. She is boundless where she is, and she is strong where she is."

Shabazz, pregnant with twins, was sitting in the audience with her four young daughters when her husband was gunned down at Harlem's Audubon Ballroom on Feb. 21, 1965. She had twin girls after his death.
One of the daughters who witnessed the murder was Qubilah Bahiyah Shabazz, then four years old.
In 1995, Qubilah was indicted on charges of plotting to kill Nation of Islam leader Louis Farrakhan, whom her mother had accused of playing a role in her husband's assassination.

Malcolm X had been Farrakhan's spiritual mentor and for many years the right-hand man and heir apparent to Elijah Muhammad, head of the Nation of Islam. But Malcolm X split with Elijah Muhammad not long before his death.
Three members of the Nation of Islam were convicted in his death.
The case against Qubilah Shabazz was dropped after she underwent counselling.

It was her son who is accused of setting the fatal fire. He was staying with his grandmother while his mother sorted out personal problems, and he was charged with juvenile delinquency after the fire.
After the death of her husband, Shabazz earned a doctorate in education. Most recently, she was a public relations administrator at Medgar Evers College in Brooklyn, New York.
She became an activist for black women and a champion for human rights, participating in the United States Aid for International Development Conference in South Africa.
She was a frequent lecturer and travelled extensively in Africa, Europe and the Caribbean. In 1995, she and Farrakhan met in Harlem in a much-publicised reconciliation.

"She leaves a legacy of love, service, dedication and caring especially for the children," said Coretta Scott King, widow of Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. "Her family has lost a mother, grandmother and a sister. The nation has lost a committed civil and human rights activist whose life and contributions have made a significant difference."
Born Betty Sanders, Shabazz grew up in Detroit and met Malcolm X at a Nation of Islam meeting in 1956.
Funeral plans were not immediately available.
